evidence.quote: Macadamia trees typically take 7-9 years to reach maturity, with yields increasing for the next 15-20 years. Flowering begins in July, and nuts begin to develop by October, with harvest season running from March through June/July (see Table 2).
evidence.doc: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS), GAIN Report SF2025-0023, 'South Africa's Macadamia Industry Grows Despite Export Uncertainty', FAS Pretoria Post, 2025

harvestMonths.notes: The report's own 'Table 2: Typical Macadamia Marketing Year in South Africa' (same page) shades 'Harvesting' across Mar-Jun with a lighter continuation into Jul, matching the text's 'March through June/July'. This is a USDA attaché (FAS) report compiling local industry (SAMAC-sourced) data, not a South African government or grower-body document itself, but was used because SAMAC's and ARC-ITSC's own cultivation pages (samac.org.za technical library, arc.agric.za/arc-itsc/Pages/Macadamia.aspx, nda.agric.za) were unreachable (503/404/membership-gated) during this research pass — see gaps.

evidence.quote: Bearing starts at 4 or 5 years, with full production in year 12.
evidence.doc: KZN DARD, Fruit and Nut Production in KZN, Macadamia bearing age

yearsToFirstCrop.notes: KZN establishment reference; this source also describes later bearing at higher elevations. Not a promise for all cultivars or every SA site.

evidence.quote: Macadamia trees typically take 7-9 years to reach maturity, with yields increasing for the next 15-20 years.
evidence.doc: USDA Foreign Agricultural Service (FAS), GAIN Report SF2025-0023, 'South Africa's Macadamia Industry Grows Despite Export Uncertainty', FAS Pretoria Post, 2025

yearsToFullBearing.notes: USDA FAS describes commercial maturity at 7–9 years while yields can continue increasing for a further 15–20 years. This does not establish a stable maximum-yield age.

evidence.quote: between 2 kg and 10 kg of nuts (Wet In Shell; WIS)
evidence.doc: SAMAC Information Hub, FAQs: potential yield at different ages

yieldKgPerTreeMature.notes: SAMAC publishes approximate age-specific output: Beaumont year 4 about 0.6–0.8 kg/tree; year 5 about 2–10 kg/tree WIS; year 8 about 16 kg/tree; possible maximum year 13–14 up to 35 kg/tree WIS. SAMAC explicitly warns these rough indicators differ between areas. Year 4 basis is not stated separately; none of these values establishes edible kernel kg or a species-wide mature forecast. Keep generic mature kg/tree null and preserve the source-specific reference.

chillUnits.notes: Macadamia is a subtropical evergreen with no documented winter-chill requirement for flowering; frost (not lack of chill) is the main cold-related limiting factor noted in South African sources (e.g. SAMAC's climate-modelling article notes an expected 'decreased frost risk, a key limiting factor for growing macadamia trees' under warming scenarios), but no source explicitly states 'no chill requirement', so left null per the rule rather than asserting it.

evidence.quote: Cross-pollination increases yields by 52% when compared with open pollination. ... Cross-pollination increases yields by 48.5% and improves nut quality (size and kernel weight). ... Genotyping of macadamia kernel to determine pollen parents: A4 was highly outcrossing (97%), 695 was 64% outcrossed, 816 41% outcrossed and 814 showed 10% outcrossing. ... Results demonstrated the critical role of honeybee colonies in macadamia orchards, with the absence of bees resulting in only 30% production in both cultivars.
evidence.doc: SAMAC (South African Macadamia Growers' Association), 'What have we learned 2024' research summary newsletter

pollination.notes: Changed from needs-cross-pollinator to partly-self-fertile in editor review: the same SAMAC summary measures 10-97% outcrossing by kernel genotyping (so some nuts are selfed) and says cross-pollination RAISES yield by about half, which is a partly self-fertile tree, not one that needs a pollinator to bear. SAMAC's own research summaries show macadamia is capable of self/open pollination (a cultivar-dependent 10-97% outcrossing rate was measured by kernel genotyping, and orchards without managed bee colonies still achieved 30% of full production) but that yield is substantially higher (48.5-52% more) with cross-pollination (interplanted cultivars) and managed honeybee colonies (industry recommends at least two hives/ha). This mixed picture — fruit set possible alone, but commercially reliant on cross-pollination/bee activity — is why 'needs-cross-pollinator' (the industry-recommended practice) rather than 'self-fertile' was chosen, though 'partly-self-fertile' is also defensible given the cultivar-dependent self/open-pollination yield floor; see this nuance rather than treating the choice as clear-cut.

supplementaryReferences.title: Macadamia output at named ages — approximate WIS references
supplementaryReferences.doc: SAMAC Information Hub, FAQs: potential yield at different ages
supplementaryReferences.note: Year 4 Beaumont: approximately 0.6–0.8 kg/tree (the year-4 basis is not explicit); year 5: 2–10 kg/tree Wet In Shell (WIS); year 8: about 16 kg/tree; year 13–14: up to 35 kg/tree WIS. SAMAC says area differences are guaranteed. This is a source reference, not a validated local schedule; it cannot seed edible kernel kg or a universal interpolated curve.

supplementaryReferences.title: Macadamia establishment depends on propagation
supplementaryReferences.quote: Grafted trees start bearing fruit as early as 3 to 5 years
supplementaryReferences.doc: SAMAC Information Hub, FAQs: time to produce nuts
supplementaryReferences.note: Grafted stock: first nuts around 3–5 years, depending on variety; seedlings usually 10–12 years and sometimes longer. SAMAC recommends removing flowers until year 3 during establishment. The existing KZN guide 4–5-year first-bearing reference remains qualified; nursery propagation must be recorded before applying it.
